---
title: "Conservative cell and environment coupling"
---

`cellerator.spatial.coupling` and the C++17 header
`Cellerator/modeling/coupling.hh` provide a concrete host exchange operator.
It couples arbitrary cell identities to finite environment compartments through
sparse weighted incidence. It assumes no tissue, cell-type or species ontology.
Its numerical state is explicitly **amount**, with concentration calculated
from caller-supplied positive volumes. This reference mechanism has no CUDA,
Torch, autograd, or scientific-validation claim.

## Contract

`ExchangePlan` keeps cell, compartment, species and link identities separate
from mutable amount and volume values. Python identities may be arbitrary
hashable values; native layouts use the existing `EntityLayout` persistent
integer IDs. The cell and compartment namespaces are distinct. Species share
an explicit order across both sides. Reordering the native arrays requires an
explicit matching layout; an array has no implicit identity lookup.

For link $e=(i,j)$ and species $s$, the requested signed amount is

$$q_{es}=\Delta t\,w_e\,[P_s(a_{is}/V_i-b_{js}/W_j)+r_{es}].$$

Positive transfer moves material from cell to environment; negative transfer
implements uptake. $P_s$ has volume/time units and $r_{es}$ has amount/time
units. The dimensionless weights are explicit and **never normalized**. A
species can have zero permeability and still have active secretion or uptake.
Distinct links may share endpoints, and their contributions add.

The operator first calculates every request from a single immutable snapshot,
then aggregates donor demand, then applies equal/opposite transfers to fresh
output state. Incoming material cannot finance another outgoing transfer in
the same step. This removes traversal-order dependence from the update law;
floating-point summation can still vary with order at roundoff scale.

The default `donor_policy="reject"` rejects aggregate demand exceeding any
donor/species amount. `donor_policy="limit"` proportionally scales **all**
outgoing requests sharing that donor/species. This changes the requested flux
law when resources run out; `ExchangeResult.limited` exposes that fact.
The signed transfer ledger exposes what actually moved. Material is conserved
per species to floating-point accuracy. No nonnegative clipping, material
creation, degradation or infinite reservoir is hidden in the operator.
An explicitly finite reservoir can be modeled as an ordinary compartment.

## Timestep and precision

`passive_dt_limit` returns the sufficient nonnegative explicit-Euler bound
$\min_{v,s} V_v/\sum_{e\ni v}w_eP_s$, ignoring zero sums. The default step
checks this bound. Active rates remain subject to the simultaneous donor budget;
the passive bound alone cannot guarantee them. Setting
`enforce_stability=False` explicitly permits steps above this bound, and usually
requires limiting. Such a step is not a claim of temporal accuracy or faithful
passive relaxation. Reduce the timestep to resolve actual dynamics.

Python is an explicit FP64 reference. Native `ExchangeState<Scalar>` supports
standard floating-point storage, using long-double multiply and accumulation
and returning the selected `Scalar` storage type. Transfer diagnostics retain
long-double precision. This particular host reference does not provide an FP16
implementation. Both routes reject invalid shapes, volumes, negative amounts,
nonfinite values and exhausted budgets under rejection mode; unrepresentable
outputs fail without mutating the input.

## Using the operator

```python
from cellerator.spatial.coupling import ExchangeLink, ExchangePlan, ExchangeState

plan = ExchangePlan(["cell"], ["bath"], ["signal"],
                    [ExchangeLink("contact", "cell", "bath")])
state = ExchangeState({"cell": [4.]}, {"bath": [0.]})
result = plan.step(state, cell_volumes={"cell": 2.},
                   compartment_volumes={"bath": 4.},
                   permeability=[1.], dt=.1)
# 0.2 amount leaves the cell and enters the bath.
assert abs(result.state.cells["cell"][0] - 3.8) < 1e-12
```

The [multicellular example](../examples/framework/extracellular_coupling.py)
uses `Model` and `StepContext` to coordinate one producer, two receivers and a
finite bath across two species. Active rates read the old bath concentration,
so receivers do not observe another cell's newly secreted material until the
next step. The run checks conserved species totals.

Existing `cellerator.spatial.diffuse` remains the graph diffusion primitive.
When composing it with exchange, callers must declare the splitting order and
choose a suitable timestep; sequential diffusion/exchange is a split method,
not a simultaneous coupled solver. In particular its scalar values are not
an unequal-volume concentration solver. No duplicate diffusion implementation
is introduced here.

Host checks live in `tests/framework/test_coupling.py` and
`tests/framework/native/coupling_test.cc`. They exercise concentration equilibrium,
unequal volumes, shared-donor capacity, simultaneous snapshots, persistent
identity reordering, species conservation and rejected invalid inputs.
